title: What actually happens when two machines talk
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe the path a message takes from one program to another across a network, name what has to be agreed in advance for it to work, and explain why the network is allowed to lose things.

blocks.text: You have spent three courses inside one machine. Everything so far — a file descriptor, a system call, a page of memory — belonged to a single computer that you could reason about completely. A network breaks that assumption in one specific way: the other end is a machine you do not control, reached over a path that can lose, delay, duplicate or reorder what you send.
The minimum that must be agreed

rows: An address — the subject of the next module
A byte order convention, and the protocol's format
Who speaks first, and what may they say?
What happens when something is lost?
The transport: TCP retransmits, UDP does not

blocks.text: Nothing on that list is optional, and none of it is discovered at run time. Two programs that disagree on any row do not communicate — they produce a hang, or a stream of bytes that means nothing to the receiver.
Byte order is agreed in advance, and it is not yours

The C course established that a machine stores a multi-byte number in its own order, and that the order differs between architectures. On a network the order is fixed by the protocol — big-endian, historically called network byte order — regardless of what either machine uses internally.

blocks.caption: Measured on a little-endian machine
lines: 8080 in network order: 1f 90      <- htons() converted it
/* Every port, every address, every length field in a header goes
through htons/htonl on the way out and ntohs/ntohl on the way in.
Forgetting one is the classic first networking bug: you connect
to port 36895 instead of 8080, and nothing is listening there. */

blocks.text: The network is allowed to fail

A packet crossing the internet passes through equipment owned by organisations you have never heard of. Any of them may drop it — because a buffer was full, because a link went down, because a routing table changed mid-flight. This is not a defect being tolerated; it is the design. Making every link reliable would be impossibly expensive, so the network offers a cheap best-effort service and lets the endpoints add reliability if they want it.

rows: Gone, and you are not told
Files, web pages, anything where a gap is corruption
Video calls, games, DNS lookups, telemetry

blocks.title: UDP is not 'TCP without the good parts'
blocks.text: For a video call, retransmitting a frame from 400 ms ago is worse than useless: it arrives too late to display, and the bandwidth it consumed delayed the current frame. UDP is the right answer when late data has no value, or when the application can do a better job of recovery than a general-purpose algorithm can. The whole of QUIC — which now carries a large share of web traffic — is built on UDP for exactly this reason.

By the end of this course you will have written a TCP server and client in C, made them handle errors properly, and then rewritten the server three ways — a thread per connection, a pool of threads, and a single thread watching many connections at once — to see where each one stops scaling. Everything before that is the knowledge needed to make those programs correct rather than merely working on your own machine.

blocks.title: Look at the connections you already have
steps: Run: ss -tunap 2>/dev/null | head -20    (every socket on this machine, with the program using it)
Identify one TCP connection and one UDP socket in that output
Run: ss -s          (a summary — how many sockets are open right now, by type)
Run: ping -c 3 1.1.1.1     and note the round-trip times and whether any packet was lost
Run: ping -c 3 -s 1400 1.1.1.1   and compare — a larger packet, the same path

Run two transfers in one curl process so its connection cache can be reused: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'first connect=%{time_connect}s total=%{time_total}s\n' https://example.com --next -s -o /dev/null -w 'second connect=%{time_connect}s total=%{time_total}s\n' https://example.com
Compare the two transfers and use curl -v to check whether the second reused a connection
Explain the difference out loud — that gap is what the rest of this course is about
blocks.expected: A list of live connections you can now name the parts of, a round-trip time that puts a number on distance, and a second curl that is faster than the first. If you cannot yet explain why, that is the correct state to start this course in — the answer involves DNS caching, connection setup, and TLS, and you will meet all three.

cheatsheet: A network adds one thing: the other end is a machine you do not control
Must be agreed in advance: address, port, byte order, protocol, failure behaviour
Network byte order is big-endian — use htons/htonl and ntohs/ntohl every time
Measured: 8080 is 90 1f in host order and 1f 90 on the wire
The network is best-effort by design: it may lose, delay, duplicate or reorder
TCP adds reliability, ordering and deduplication; UDP adds nothing
UDP is right when late data is worthless — video, games, DNS, telemetry
ss -tunap lists sockets; ping measures round trip; curl -w times the phases

checkpoint.prompt: A program sends a port number without calling htons. What is the likely symptom?

choices.A: Nothing — modern hardware handles both byte orders
choices.C: It connects to a different port

checkpoint.explanation: The bytes were interpreted in the other order. Verified: 8080 is 90 1f in host order and 1f 90 on the wire. Send the host-order bytes and the far end reads a different number entirely, so nothing is listening there.

checkpoint.prompt: Why would a video call use UDP when TCP guarantees delivery?

choices.C: Retransmitted data arrives too late to matter
choices.D: UDP is simply faster for every kind of application traffic

checkpoint.explanation: Reliability is only valuable if late data still has value. When it does not, retransmission spends bandwidth and adds delay for nothing. The retransmitted frame cannot be displayed in time, and waiting for it delays the frame being shown now.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is the network allowed to drop packets rather than being built to never do so?

choices.A: Delivery guarantees at every hop would cost too much
choices.B: It is a bug that has not been fixed
choices.D: Packets are dropped only when the network is under attack

checkpoint.explanation: The network is cheap and best-effort and the endpoints add reliability if they need it. This is the end-to-end principle: keep the middle simple and fast, and put the features that only some applications need at the edges. Guaranteeing delivery at every hop would be prohibitively expensive.

checkpoint.prompt: You load the same page again and it is faster. Which option is a routing change rather than a cache or reuse mechanism?

choices.B: The route through the internet became shorter
choices.D: An existing connection from the first load was reused

checkpoint.explanation: A shorter route is possible after routing or CDN changes, but it is not a cache or reuse mechanism. DNS caching, TLS resumption and connection reuse are three distinct mechanisms covered later in this course.
